div.div:
Multi-Attach: The "Shared Drive" Trap
Most EBS volumes can only be plugged into one EC2 instance at a time. Multi-Attach allows a volume to be plugged into up to 16 instances simultaneously.

div.div: The "Application-Level" Warning: Just because two servers are plugged into the same drive doesn't mean they know how to share.

div.div: You must use a "Clustered Filesystem" (like GFS2) or an application that handles its own distributed locking. EBS does not do this for you.

div.div: ext4 : It is extremely reliable and handles directories with millions of small files very efficiently. If you are running a web server with many small images or logs, ext4 is great

div.div: XFS : XFS was designed for high-performance and large files. It excels at "Parallel I/O," meaning it can handle multiple CPU cores writing to the same disk simultaneously without getting "locked up."

div.div: Default (4KB): If you write a 1KB file, it still takes up 4KB of space. This is efficient for small files but creates a lot of metadata (paperwork) for large files.

div.div: Large Blocks (16KB or 64KB): By increasing the block size, you reduce the "paperwork" the CPU has to do to track where data is stored.

div.div: For a large sequential database (like a Data Warehouse), 64KB is faster. However, if your database writes in 4KB chunks (like standard PostgreSQL), using a 16KB filesystem block size can cause "Write Amplification," where the disk does more work than necessary.

div.div: noatime (No Access Time): By default, Linux records the exact time every time a file is read.

div.div: For a database that reads thousands of blocks per second, this creates thousands of tiny, useless writes. noatime turns this off, saving disk bandwidth.

div.div: data=writeback (ext4 journaling mode): only metadata is journaled, and file data may be written to disk after the metadata that points to it.

div.div: It is faster, but after a crash a file can contain stale or garbage blocks. Most production DBs keep the default data=ordered and rely on their own Write-Ahead Log (WAL) + fsync for durability.
